frictionVectors.title: European energy balancing
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over its gas sector while expanding European export ties. Demand for additional supply and infrastructure investment creates leverage for outside partners without removing state primacy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya pressures Algeria’s borders and complicates its non-interventionist security posture. Cross-border militant and smuggling networks remain a persistent sovereignty risk.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting competing United States, European, and Chinese interest because of its access to Central African minerals. The investment can improve connectivity but may constrain Luanda’s room to maneuver over logistics and resource flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil still dominates export earnings and public finances, leaving Angola exposed to price cycles and foreign technical capital. Diversification efforts have not yet displaced the extractive structure of the economy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to sanctions legacies, border closures, and disputes over access through Benin’s port infrastructure. These tensions directly affect regional commerce and Benin’s leverage as a coastal gateway.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization, export corridors, and energy projects depend heavily on external finance and operators. Benin is gaining capacity but must manage the risk that strategic infrastructure serves outside commercial priorities more than domestic industrialization.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers relationship reset
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater control over marketing and beneficiation. Negotiations with De Beers test the country’s ability to convert mineral dependence into durable sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: New minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Interest in uranium, copper, and other critical minerals is expanding the investor field beyond diamonds. The main risk is reproducing an enclave model in which foreign capital captures value while local processing remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign influence over security and mining
frictionVectors.details: The junta’s rejection of traditional Western partnerships and closer engagement with Russia aim to increase strategic autonomy, but they also create new dependencies in arms, security services, and political support. Security needs increasingly shape access to mining zones and external concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal gold control
frictionVectors.details: Gold is central to state revenue and sovereignty messaging, yet informal production, smuggling, and insecurity limit effective government control. Conflict-affected mining areas remain vulnerable to armed-group taxation and opaque external networks.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and rare-earth development
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects offer revenue and infrastructure but risk limiting Burundi's control over licensing, processing, and export value. Weak institutions constrain effective oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-border tensions
frictionVectors.details: Political and security tensions with Rwanda complicate trade, border management, and regional resource cooperation, while instability in eastern DRC adds pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde benefits from cooperation with the United States, Europe, and regional partners on maritime surveillance, but this also creates dependence on external security infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment dominates tourism, ports, and energy projects. The model supports growth but leaves the country exposed to external capital, imported fuel, and demand shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas, and mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon and mineral projects depend heavily on foreign capital and technical operators, limiting domestic value capture and increasing governance risks around concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-affected infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Anglophone conflict and insecurity in the Far North threaten transport corridors, agricultural supply chains, and energy infrastructure while increasing reliance on external contractors and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: The state has limited control over dispersed mining zones, where armed groups, foreign traders, and security-linked commercial networks compete for rents and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and resource alignment
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on Russian-linked security support has strengthened regime protection but may trade short-term security for opaque resource arrangements and reduced bargaining autonomy.

highlights: Sahel and Sudan insecurity constrict autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and oil dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's principal oil exports rely on infrastructure and commercial arrangements connected to Cameroon, leaving revenue security vulnerable to external operators, transit risks, and price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security patrons
frictionVectors.details: Instability along the Sudanese and Libyan fronts drives reliance on foreign military, financial, and diplomatic partners, complicating sovereign control over borderlands and strategic decisions.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to reject French sovereignty over Mayotte, while France controls the island's migration regime, maritime access, and substantial economic resources.

frictionVectors.title: DEPENDENCE ON EXTERNAL FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic revenue and infrastructure capacity leave Comoros reliant on foreign aid, remittances, and externally financed ports, energy, and telecommunications.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACTS AND CRITICAL MINERALS
frictionVectors.details: Copper, cobalt, and other strategic minerals draw intense Chinese, Western, and regional competition, while contract transparency and domestic value capture remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONFLICT AND BORDER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border tensions involving Rwanda continue to undermine Kinshasa's control over mineral-rich eastern territories and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign oil companies remain central to production and technical capacity, leaving the state exposed to price volatility and limiting domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND DEBT LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, telecoms, and other projects expand connectivity but increase reliance on external contractors, creditors, and resource-backed financing.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding local processing and regulatory leverage, but multinational traders and volatile global prices still constrain national value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The Abidjan and San Pedro corridors are attracting Gulf, Chinese, European, and regional investment as Côte d'Ivoire balances commercial openness with greater security autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: BASE AND PORT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's strategic autonomy and intensify great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND LOGISTICS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure and reliance on Ethiopia-linked transit revenues create exposure to debt servicing pressures and shifts in regional trade access.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and Gulf investment provide essential liquidity but constrain policy autonomy and expand foreign influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Suez traffic faces regional disruption, while the GERD dispute with Ethiopia continues to shape Egypt's water-security planning.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, imported expertise, and difficult new offshore investments.

frictionVectors.title: External asset exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors remain important to infrastructure delivery, while opaque governance limits domestic capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide foreign exchange but expose Eritrea to external operators, sanctions risk, and commodity-price volatility.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Ethiopia and Red Sea security keep transport corridors vulnerable and limit broader economic normalization.

frictionVectors.title: SACU revenue exposure
frictionVectors.details: Customs receipts and supply chains remain heavily tied to South Africa, leaving national budgeting vulnerable to regional downturns and policy shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and energy reliance
frictionVectors.details: Electricity, transport, and industrial inputs depend substantially on cross-border systems, limiting independent resource-security options.

highlights: Debt and port access constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Nile and regional water diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The GERD increases Ethiopia's strategic leverage but continues to generate acute friction with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and data sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for reliable Red Sea trade access give external creditors, Gulf actors, and neighboring states significant influence over Ethiopia's economic choices.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese, iron ore, and other minerals while balancing established French, Chinese, and other investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors and port capacity remain vulnerable to foreign financing and operational influence, limiting Gabon's ability to fully capture value from its resource base.

highlights: Fisheries and cashew exports face external pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese security and border footprint
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal and regional security mechanisms for strategic protection, constraining independent foreign-policy and border-management choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets and weak enforcement threaten coastal livelihoods and food security, with licensing transparency and surveillance remaining persistent sovereignty concerns.

highlights: Gold and lithium sovereignty under debate

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains the core export earner, but refining, trading, and financing are heavily shaped by external actors; emerging lithium projects have intensified demands for domestic processing and stronger state participation.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental stress
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey damages water systems and agricultural land while exposing gaps in state enforcement, local patronage, and oversight of both domestic and foreign-linked mining networks.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and other foreign capital, rail, and port commitments; Guinea is gaining infrastructure but remains exposed to unequal bargaining and enclave-style extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite dependence and political centralization
frictionVectors.details: Bauxite exports generate revenue without sufficient domestic processing, while the junta's concentrated decision-making weakens transparency over concessions, contracts, and local-content obligations.

highlights: Fragile civilian rule survives elite rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Cashew-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Guinea-Bissau exports most cashews with limited domestic processing, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to foreign buyers, price shocks, and port bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Transnational trafficking networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and porous maritime routes sustain cocaine-transit risks, creating external leverage over political and security elites and undermining sovereign control of coastal infrastructure.

highlights: Regional logistics hub under fiscal pressure
Balancing China, Gulf, and Western partnerships

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures constrain Nairobi's bargaining power with international lenders and external infrastructure financiers. Control and commercial access around Mombasa and the Lamu corridor remain strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals positioning
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking investment in minerals and energy while attempting to preserve domestic value capture. Competition among Western, Chinese, Gulf, and regional investors creates regulatory and sovereignty risks.

highlights: Economy remains structurally tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide strategic revenue but deepen dependence on South African infrastructure, financing, and downstream demand. Delays, cost overruns, and disputes over project governance can weaken sovereign returns.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and customs vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Manufacturing and customs revenues remain exposed to external trade preferences and South African economic conditions. Limited diversification leaves policy space vulnerable to outside commercial pressure.

highlights: Ports and corridors attract competing investors

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession leverage
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations and proposed expansion give foreign mining firms substantial influence over transport, employment, and fiscal policy. Liberia faces pressure to secure better local processing, revenue transparency, and infrastructure benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and transport corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and mineral-export corridors are becoming more important to external investors and regional trade strategies. Weak state capacity increases the risk that concession-linked infrastructure serves exporters more than the broader economy.

highlights: Oil remains hostage to political fragmentation
Foreign security patrons shape national access

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use production, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. Disruptions or opaque arrangements threaten the National Oil Corporation's autonomy and national revenue stability.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf actors, and European states retain overlapping security and energy interests in Libya. External backing of domestic factions limits unified sovereignty over ports, bases, migration routes, and hydrocarbons.

highlights: Mining corridors outpace domestic value capture
Energy and food insecurity constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Madagascar is seeking greater fiscal and processing benefits but remains exposed to investor pressure and commodity-price swings.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and weak transport links limit domestic industrialization and increase reliance on external financiers and operators. Port, mining, and power investments can improve capacity while also concentrating strategic control outside the state.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign capital for uranium, graphite, and rare-earth projects while seeking stronger state participation and local processing. Limited fiscal capacity weakens its negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Imported Energy Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Fuel and electricity shortages remain vulnerable to foreign-exchange scarcity and regional supply disruptions, constraining industrial and agricultural sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Renegotiation Risk
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign mining operators for higher state revenues, local beneficiation, and stronger regulatory control. Disputes with major operators could reduce investment and production.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Mali's reliance on Russian security support provides regime protection but creates dependence over operational access, payments, and strategic infrastructure. Persistent insurgency continues to threaten mining corridors.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but exposes Mauritania to foreign operator control, cross-border coordination risks, and disputes over revenue transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Extractives Logistics Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and future gas exports rely on foreign capital, port capacity, rail infrastructure, and multinational technical expertise. This limits near-term domestic value capture despite strong state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Implementation Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement over the Chagos Archipelago and continued operation of the Diego Garcia base remain sensitive to UK-US security interests. Implementation terms could constrain Mauritius's practical control over the territory.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control over its economy, but tourism, financial services, and infrastructure remain exposed to shifts in foreign capital, regulation, and strategic competition.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding phosphate, fisheries, port, and renewable-energy infrastructure in Western Sahara while facing legal and diplomatic challenges over resource consent and territorial status.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Balancing
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and US investment supports ports, energy, and manufacturing but creates competing external leverage. Rabat is managing this through diversified partnerships and state-linked investment vehicles.

highlights: Cabo Delgado LNG remains strategically delayed
Natural-gas wealth faces security and governance risks

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led LNG dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain major influence over Mozambique's offshore gas projects, while delays and security costs limit state control over revenues and timelines.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten gas infrastructure, local communities, and transport corridors despite Mozambican, Rwandan, and regional security efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of emerging hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate exploration and development of Namibia's offshore oil prospects, creating future risks over taxation, local content, and revenue sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and water constraints
frictionVectors.details: Green-hydrogen and port projects depend heavily on foreign finance and technology, while limited water, power, and transport capacity may constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and mining renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is pressing foreign mining interests for greater national control and revenue, increasing uncertainty around existing concessions and investment.

frictionVectors.title: Oil pipeline dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports rely on cross-border infrastructure through Benin, leaving its resource strategy exposed to diplomatic disputes, border insecurity, and external transit control.

frictionVectors.title: Multinational oil legacy
frictionVectors.details: International operators still influence upstream production and technical capacity, while disputes over environmental damage, divestments, and contract terms limit perceived sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and insecurity gap
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline vandalism, crude theft, grid weakness, and insurgency continue to erode public control over energy assets despite expanded domestic refining capacity.

highlights: Mineral value chains remain externally exposed
Regional security posture drives economic friction

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's position in regional tin, tantalum, and tungsten supply chains faces persistent international scrutiny over traceability and alleged links to conflict minerals from eastern Congo.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo security entanglement
frictionVectors.details: Accusations of support for M23 and tensions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo risk sanctions, aid pressure, and disruption of regional trade and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea security
frictionVectors.details: Limited naval capacity leaves São Tomé and Príncipe reliant on regional partners and external patrol support to protect its waters and fisheries.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing exposure
frictionVectors.details: Prospective hydrocarbon blocks attract foreign operators and political expectations, while weak fiscal and regulatory capacity limits bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Oil and gas production with international firms offers revenue and export leverage, but contract terms, local-content demands, and revenue transparency remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Regional gas interdependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project ties Senegal's energy strategy to Mauritania and foreign operators, creating exposure to cross-border governance and infrastructure risks.

frictionVectors.title: External maritime dependence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on partners such as India, France, and other international actors for maritime surveillance, anti-piracy support, and protection of its vast exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on tourism, imported energy, and external finance constrains economic sovereignty and leaves infrastructure planning vulnerable to outside lenders and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations provide exports and jobs but leave the state exposed to foreign ownership, commodity cycles, and disputes over taxes, royalties, and local benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: External financing and investment in ports, roads, and mining corridors can improve connectivity while reinforcing long-term dependence on foreign commercial and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented offshore licensing
frictionVectors.details: Federal and subnational disputes over offshore hydrocarbons complicate licensing, revenue sharing, and enforcement, creating openings for foreign operators and political patrons.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized security architecture
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, the African Union, and Western partners remain central to Somalia's security infrastructure, limiting independent control over ports, bases, and maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Access
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and control over platinum-group metals, manganese and other critical minerals while balancing investment pressure from China, the United States and Europe.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Logistics Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion and rail failures continue to weaken sovereign control over mineral exports and increase dependence on external capital and technical partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Transit Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese pipelines and export terminals, leaving its main revenue stream vulnerable to Sudan's war, infrastructure disruption and politically controlled transit arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Regional states, oil operators and international donors retain substantial influence because state institutions remain weak and armed competition continues to threaten transport corridors and production zones.

highlights: Red Sea access gains strategic value

frictionVectors.title: War Economy and Gold
frictionVectors.details: Competing military networks and foreign-linked commercial actors exploit gold and other revenues, reducing central state control and financing continued conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Sudan's Red Sea infrastructure and overland routes are increasingly contested by regional powers seeking influence over trade, arms access and future reconstruction.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Project Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing foreign mining companies for higher state participation, local processing and revenue transparency while competing investors seek access to gold, graphite and critical minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Strategic Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam and rail links strengthens Tanzania's regional leverage, but Chinese, Gulf and Western financing interests create pressure over control, debt exposure and operating rights.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hinge

frictionVectors.title: Port and Transit Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a key gateway for landlocked Sahel markets, increasing exposure to foreign logistics operators, customs interests and shifting regional trade alignments.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability near the northern frontier are testing Togo's security capacity and could draw deeper dependence on external intelligence, arms and border-support networks.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. The arrangement strengthens short-term fiscal resilience but narrows sovereign room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported gas and electricity, particularly through interconnection and supply arrangements involving Algeria and Europe. Delayed renewable investment and weak public finances limit diversification.

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil financing and transit
frictionVectors.details: The Tilenga project and the East African Crude Oil Pipeline promise major export revenues but remain vulnerable to financing constraints, environmental opposition, and geopolitical pressure. Uganda's dependence on foreign operators and the Tanzanian export route limits full control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and contractors remain important in roads, power, and industrial infrastructure. Debt-servicing obligations and project concentration can reduce Kampala's bargaining flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting investment from Gulf, Western, and Chinese firms, but foreign ownership and limited domestic refining capacity leave the country exposed to external pricing and processing decisions. The push for local beneficiation is politically popular but financially difficult.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor restructuring are improving fiscal credibility while constraining policy choices. Transport, power, and mining investment remain dependent on external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign firms dominate major mineral projects, giving outside actors strong influence over extraction, processing, and export channels. Zimbabwe's beneficiation ambitions are slowed by unreliable power, capital shortages, and regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted financing, and disputed governance continue to push Harare toward alternative partners, especially China and Gulf investors. This diversification reduces Western leverage but can deepen opaque concessionary deals and extractive dependence.
